full_judgment:
4. Both sides adduced oral and documentary evidence in support of their respective cases. The learned Munsif upon a consideration of the same dismissed the suit holding that the suits were not maintainable being hit by Section 21 of the Public Demands Recovery Act. The learned Munsif further found that the alleged agreements could not be established and disbelieved the receipts filed by the plaintiffs in support of the said agreements. The learned Munsif further held that there was no independent or disinterested witness to support the plaintiffs' case and the defendant as the successful bidder had purchased the property in auction sale with his own money for his own benefit. The learned Munsif further found that the signatures on the receipts having been totally denied by the defendant, the onus was on the plaintiffs to prove the same. Although the signatures were sent to the Handwriting expert for his opinion and the some was also obtained, the plaintiffs did not take any step to examine the Handwriting expert and bring it into evidence and as such he held that the presumption must necessarily be adverse to the plaintiffs so far as the signatures were concerned. Upon these findings the learned Munsif totally disbelieved the plaintiff's case and dismissed the suits. 

 8. Mr. Huq next assailed the finding of the learned Subordinate Judge with regard to the opinion of the Handwriting expert. It appears that the signatures on the receipts which have been marked as Exhibit 1 series were seriously challenged by the defendant who categorically denied having ever signed such receipts. At the, instance of the plaintiffs the signatures along with the specimen signatures of the defendant were sent to the Handwriting expert for his opinion which was duly obtained but thereafter the opinion was not brought into evidence by the plaintiffs by calling the Handwriting expert and as such the learned Munsif drew adverse presumption against the plaintiffs in this regard. The learned Subordinate Judge however in reversing the finding of the learned Munsif has held that he was of the definite opinion that the signatures in the receipts were in the hand of the defendant. At the same time, he has observed that the Handwriting expert opined against the plaintiffs and that plaintiff Nizamuddin also filed objection against the expert's opinion. He also does not say that he has examined the signatures himself. Curiously enough, the, learned Subordinate Judge did not think it necessary to assign any reason for coming to this abrupt finding. Law enjoins that the appellate court must give reasons whether affirming or reversing a finding and it is more so, when he is reversing it. Having regard to these facts and circumstances, I find that the trial court was perfectly justified in drawing adverse presumption against the plaintiffs for withholding the expert's opinion from the court and that the signatures could not be proved to be those of the defendant.
